newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Sell JGBs on any Tankan rally.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Sell JGBs on any Tankan rally.

text.p: Japanese government bonds (JGBs) may get a temporary lift from the quarterly Tankan report this week but speculation of higher interest rates will return to bite the market, analysts said on Monday.
Longer term, the market could revive if the yen takes off again, they said.

"The market is relatively well supported near term," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International in London. "As we get evidence of a stronger economy and of rates going up, there could be some sell off in the market and therefore higher yields."

The Bank of Japan's Tankan survey of corporate sentiment on Wednesday was widely expected to show weakened economic growth in the second quarter allaying recent market concerns a Japanese interest rate rise was on the way.
A Reuters consensus of economists forecasts expected sentiment on major manufacturing to fall 0.8 compared with a 2.0 rise previously.
Joanne Collins, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London, said JGBs had shown little reaction to the recent weakness of the yen and were awaiting the Tankan report.

"If the Tankan is in line with expectations, we are looking for JGBs to strengthen a little bit but we recommend investors sell into that strength because we don't see it either being sustainable or extending much further," she said.
She said despite an anticipated gradual firming of the yen in the next few months, Japanese investors should look to invest elsewhere.
"We are looking for outperformance of the U.S. market against the core European markets so that is the obvious, and the easiest, place for Japanese investors to go."
But Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London, was more positive on JGBs.
Shah said the dollar/yen rate could strengthen further on a weak Tankan report but in the medium to long-term he was positive on the yen.
"We think that even if the JGB market does fall it is probably worth buying the market from a currency perspective," he said.

At 1337 GMT, the dollar/yen was at 115.44/115.54, just below the highs of 115.67 seen in early Europe after the G7 nations conference in Denver over the weekend played down Japan's rising trade surplus.
Shah added there had been so much convergence in global bond yields that the biggest value in portfolio performance would come from foreign exchange exposure.

Taking the Italian market as an example, he said if Japanese interest rates did go up, the yen would benefit, sending the dollar weaker against the mark, and the mark in turn stronger against European currencies.
"So from an Italian point of view it makes sense to have a slightly higher exposure to the yen," he said.
JGBs also looked attractive from a risk/reward perspective, Shah said.
"You could see a three point decline in JGBs but equally if the EMU bandwagon receives a setback in Europe BTPs can easily fall by three, four, five points," he said.
